Meccan, and it has fifty-two verses [revealed after Al-Alaq]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

It has been read as "Nun, wal-qalam" with clear pronunciation (bayan) and with assimilation (idgham), and with the nun vowelless, fatha-vowelled, and kasra-vowelled, as in "Sad." The intended meaning is this letter of the alphabet (huruf al-mu'jam). As for their claim that it is an inkwell (dawah), I do not know whether this is a lexical (lughawi) or a legal (shar'i) usage.

If it is the name of an inkwell, it cannot be free of being either a common noun (jins) or a proper name ('alam). If it is a common noun, where is the i'rab (case inflection) and the tanwin (nunation)? If it is a proper name, where is the i'rab? Either way, it must have a position within the composition of the sentence. If you say that it is an oath-object (muqsam bihi), then if it is a common noun it must be in the genitive and nunated, and the oath would be by an indefinite, unknown inkwell, as if it were said: "By an inkwell and the pen." And if it is a proper name, you must either make it diptotic (sarf) and genitive, or leave it undeclined and put it in the accusative because of its being a proper name and feminine. Likewise the interpretation as "the fish" is either to mean the letter nun of "al-ninan" (whale), or to make it a proper name for the Leviathan (al-Yahmut) which they claim [the reading in the note: "or to make it a proper name for al-Yahmut" perhaps with a ba' as in other commentators' wording, so let it be verified (ʿ)]. Likewise the interpretation as a tablet of light or gold, and the river in Paradise, and the like.

He swore by the pen to honour it, because of what is in its creation and its ordering from the evidence of great wisdom, and because of the benefits and advantages in it that description cannot encompass. "And what they inscribe" (wa-ma yasturun): what is written of books. It has been said: what the guardian angels (al-hafazah) record. "Ma" is either relative (mawsulah) or verbal-infinitival (masdariyyah). It is permissible to mean by "the pen" its possessors, so that the pronoun in "yasturun" refers to them, as if it were said: "and the possessors of the pen and their writings," or "and their lines of writing," and by them is meant everything that is inscribed, or the guardian angels.

If you ask, "To what does the *bāʾ* in *bi-niʿmati rabbika* (بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ) relate, and what is its grammatical position (*maḥall*)?" I answer: it relates to *majnūn* (مجنون) in its negated form [[In al-Nasafi, it is said to relate to an omitted element, and its position is accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). The governing word for both is *bi-majnūn*. (Editor)]], just as it relates to *ʿāqil* (عاقل) in its affirmed form in your saying, "You are, by God's grace, sensible (*anta bi-niʿmati llāhi ʿāqil*)." Affirmation and negation are equal in this, as in your saying, "Zayd struck ʿAmr" and "Zayd did not strike ʿAmr." The verb governs in affirmation and in negation with a single mode of government. Its position is accusative as a circumstantial state, as if he had said, "You are not a madman, bestowing favour upon yourself by that" [[The phrase "bestowing favour upon yourself by that" is in al-Nasafi, after what precedes it: *anta bi-niʿmati rabbika*, i.e., by His bestowal upon you of prophethood and other things. This is the referent of the demonstrative. (Editor)]]. The *bāʾ* does not prevent *majnūn* from governing what precedes it, because it is superfluous, added for emphasis of the negation.

The meaning is the dismissal of what the Meccan unbelievers attributed to him out of enmity and envy, and that his soundness of intellect and the magnanimity required by his qualification for prophethood are from God's bestowal upon him. [[The phrase "and that it is from God's bestowal upon him of soundness" is probably "from God's bestowal upon him of soundness of intellect," i.e., its firmness, as the *Ṣiḥāḥ* states. (Editor)]]

"And surely for you there is a reward" (*wa-inna laka la-ajran*), i.e., a recompense, "for bearing that and swallowing its bitterness and being patient with it," "unending" (*ghayra mamnūn*), i.e., not cut off, like His words, "a gift not cut off" (*ʿaṭāʾan ghayra majdhūdh*), or "not bestowed upon you as a favour." [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its meaning is not cut off, like His words, 'a gift not cut off'..." Ahmad [Ibn al-Munayyir] said: The Prophet (ﷺ) would not have been pleased with al-Zamakhshari's explanation of the verse in this way. He (ﷺ) said, "None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said, "Not even you, Messenger of God?" He said, "Not even I, unless God covers me with His grace and mercy." Al-Zamakhshari's ill manners have reached a point that requires the legal penalty (ḥadd). The sum of his statement is that God has no favour upon anyone and no grace in entering Paradise, because a person has merely performed what is obligatory upon him. We seek refuge in God from audacity towards Him. (Editor's note: Ahmad's remark here.)]] This is because it is a reward that you deserve for your deed, and not an initial bounty. Favours are only bestowed upon, not rewards for deeds.

The greatness of his character lay in his great forbearance toward the painful things (al-mamdiyat) [[His saying "ihtimalihi al-mamdiyat" means: the painful things. The one who is afflicted (al-mafun) means the madman, because he is afflicted (futin), that is, tested, by madness. Or because the Arabs claimed that he was possessed by the jinn, and the jinn are those who afflict the one who is struck by them among them. The preposition bi (in ﴿بأيكم﴾) is superfluous. Or al-mafun is a verbal noun (masdar), like al-ma'qul and al-majlud, meaning: which of you is the madness? Or: which of the two groups among you is the madness? [[His words "or which of the two groups among you is the madness" is perhaps "the madman." In al-Nasafi: al-Zajjaj said: the bi here means fi (in). ﴿So do not obey the deniers.﴾ This is an incitement and a spur to firmness in opposing them. They had wanted him to worship God for a period and their gods for a period, and to spare him their harms in return. ﴿Had you been pliant﴾, that is, had you been soft and conciliatory, ﴿they would have been pliant﴾.

If you ask: why is ﴿fayudhinun﴾ (they would be pliant) in the nominative and not in the subjunctive by implying "an" (that), though it is the answer to a wish? I answer: it has been diverted to another construction, namely that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "so they are pliant." Like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever believes in his Lord, then he fears no [loss]﴾, meaning: they wish you would be pliant, so they are pliant then. Or: they wish for your pliancy, so they are now pliant, out of their hope for your pliancy. **Ḥallāf**: one who swears often, whether in truth or in falsehood. Such a fault is enough of a deterrent for one who is accustomed to swearing. Similar to it is His saying, ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle to your oaths﴾.

**Mahīn**: from *al-muhāna*, which means paucity and lowliness. He means paucity of judgment and discernment. Or he meant the liar, because he is contemptible among people.

**Hammāz**: a slanderer, a defamer, a stabber (with the tongue).

From al-Ḥasan: *yalwī shidqayhi*, he twists his cheeks (in mockery) at the backs of people.

**Mashshā'in bi-namīm**: one who carries tales, transmitting speech from one people to another, with the intent of stirring up mischief and discord between them. *Al-namīm* and *al-namīmah* mean incitement and tale-bearing. (Al-Sihāḥ says: "*al-tadrīb bayn al-qawm*" means stirring enmity.) (ʿ)

Some Arabs recited to me:

*"Flare up, as the tale-bearing flares up,*
*Walking with it, Zahrā, to Tamīm."*

This is said by a Bedouin addressing the fire. *Al-tashabbub* means kindling. *Al-tamīmah* means the distortion and embellishment of speech to cause discord among people. A garment that is *munammam* or *munamnam* is one decorated with patterns or made fine. Zahrā, with a fatḥah, is the name of a tale-bearing woman. Tamīm is the tribe of Tamīm. He made the fire occupy the place of a reasonable being, commanded it, and said: "Flare up like the flaring of tale-bearing, while this woman walks with it to the Banū Tamīm." She was very active in causing discord among the Arabs, so that she became proverbial. He made the flaring of her tale-bearing more intense than the flaring of fire, so he commanded it to blaze as she blazes. Between *namīm* and *tamīmah* there is *jinās lāḥiq* (a near-paronomasia). (ʿ)

**Mannāʿ lil-khayr**: stingy. *Al-khayr* means wealth. Or *mannāʿ* means one who withholds the good for his family, and the good is Islam. So he mentioned the one prevented from it instead of the thing prevented, as if he said: "one who withholds from the good."

It is said he is al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra al-Makhzūmī. He was wealthy and had ten sons. He would say to them and to his kin: "Whoever among you embraces Islam, I will withhold my bounty from him."

From Ibn ʿAbbās: he is Abū Jahl.

From Mujāhid: al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth.

From al-Suddī: al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, whose origin was among Thaqīf, but whose affiliation was with Zuhra. For this reason it is said he is a *zanīm*.

**Muʿtadin**: exceeding the bounds in wrongdoing.

**Athīm**: much sinful, committing many sins.

**ʿUtull**: harsh, coarse, rough. From *ʿatalahu*: when one drags him with violence and roughness.

**Baʿda dhālika**: after he was described with the defects and shortcomings mentioned above.

**Zanīm**: an illegitimate, adopted one. (The author Maḥmūd said: "*al-ʿutull* is the coarse one, and *al-zanīm* is the illegitimate claimant. Likewise al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra was adopted by al-Mughīra eighteen years after his birth…" Aḥmad said: "He took these two to be the worst of his defects from his words *baʿda dhālik*, for it indicates a distance in rank between what was mentioned first and what was mentioned after it, in evil and in good. Its counterpart in good is His saying: ﴿and the angels after that are supporters﴾. For this reason *thumma* is used to express the distance in ranks, even though it gives the reverse of the existential order.") (ʿ)

Ḥassān said:

*"You are a zanīm, hung to the family of Hāshim,*
*As a lone arrow is hung behind the rider."*

This is addressed by Ḥassān ibn Thābit to al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra. He says that he is *zanīm*, that is, attached to the family of Hāshim like the *zunmah* on a hide, which is a small piece of skin left hanging at its edge. He compared him to it, and compared him to the empty, lone arrow hung behind the rider. (ʿ)

Al-Walīd was an adopted outsider among the Quraysh, not of their stock. His father claimed him eighteen years after his birth.

It is also said: his mother committed adultery, and this was not known until this verse was revealed. He made his coarseness and his being claimed by another the worst of his defects, because when a man is coarse and his nature is harsh, his heart hardens and he becomes bold in every sin. Also, the general rule is that when the seed is corrupt, what comes from it is corrupt.

For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The child of fornication will not enter Paradise, nor his child, nor his child's child." (Abū Nuʿaym narrated it in the biography of Mujāhid, through ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥasan, in the biography of Yūsuf ibn Asbāṭ, through Barakah ibn Muḥammad, from Yūsuf ibn Asbāṭ, from Abū Isrāʾīl al-Malāʾī, from Ismāʿīl ibn Isḥāq, from Qabīṣah ibn ʿAmr, from Mujāhid, from Banī ʿUmar, from Abū Hurayrah. Then he narrated it through Isḥāq ibn Manṣūr from Abū Isrāʾīl with the same wording, but Abū Isrāʾīl is extremely weak. Ibn Ṭāhir and Ibn al-Jawzī claimed that this hadith is fabricated. It has been contradicted on the authority of Mujāhid: al-Nasāʾī narrated it through Ibrāhīm ibn Mujāhid, from Mujāhid, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Abū Hurayrah, with the wording: "The child of fornication will not enter Paradise, nor anything of his offspring up to seven fathers," but Ibrāhīm is weak in it. He also narrated it through Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād, from Mujāhid, from Abū Saʿīd, similar to the hadith of Manṣūr that follows, but Yazīd is weak. Al-Nasāʾī also narrated through Shuʿbah, from Manṣūr, from Sālim ibn Abī al-Jaʿd, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sharīk, from Jābān, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, with the wording: "The child of an adulteress will not enter Paradise," and through Sufyān, from Manṣūr, dropping ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sharīk. Ibn Ḥibbān narrated it through both channels, and said: "Both channels are preserved, but al-Thawrī is more knowledgeable about the hadith of Manṣūr.")

**Baʿda dhālik** is similar to *thumma* in His saying: ﴿then he was among those who believed﴾.

Al-Ḥasan read *ʿutullin* with a *ḍammah* (in the nominative), as a form of disparagement. This reading strengthens what is indicated by what comes after.

**Zanīm**: from *al-zunmah*, which is a small piece of flesh from a she-goat's hide, cut off and left hanging from its throat. He is an addition hung on someone who does not belong to him.

**An kāna dhā māl**: this is connected to His saying: ﴿and do not obey﴾. That is, do not obey him with these defects, because he possesses wealth. That is, because of his prosperity and his share of this world. It is also permissible that it be connected to what follows, meaning: because he is wealthy and is supported by sons ﴿who denies Our signs﴾. (The phrase "who denies Our signs" is in al-Nasafī's wording: "denies with Our signs." ʿ) It is not governed by *qāla* (he says), which is the answer of *idhā* (when), because what follows a conditional does not govern what precedes it. Rather, what governs it is the meaning of denial that the sentence indicates.

It is read *a-an kāna*? (with the interrogative hamzah), as an interrogation: "Is it because he possesses wealth and sons that he denies?" Or: "Would you obey him because he possesses wealth?"

Al-Zubayrī narrated from Nāfiʿ: *in kāna* with a kasrah, with the conditional applied to the addressee. That is: do not obey every oath-maker who stipulates his prosperity, because if you obey the disbeliever for his wealth, it is as if you made wealth a condition for obedience. Diverting the conditional to the addressee is like diverting the expectation (*tarajjī*) to him in His saying: ﴿perhaps he will be reminded﴾.

**The nose** (*al-wajh*, the face, the nose): The nose is the most honored part of the body, and the nose is the most honored part of the face because it is foremost in it. For this reason they made it the place of honor and zeal, and derived from it *al-anfah* (pride). They said: "The nose is in the nose," "he protected his nose," and "so-and-so has a lofty nose." And for the humiliated they said: "his nose was slit," and "his nose was rubbed in the dust." So he expressed the utmost humiliation and disgrace by branding on the snout, because a mark on the face is a disfigurement and a debasement. How much more so when it is on the most honored part of it! The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) branded al-ʿAbbās's camels on their faces, and he said to him: "Honor the faces." (I have not seen it in this exact form. In Ibn Ḥibbān, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, that al-ʿAbbās branded a camel of his and a beast on its face, and the Prophet (ﷺ) saw it and was angry. Al-ʿAbbās said: "I will not brand it except at its far end." So he branded it on its buttocks. Its origin is in Muslim with the wording: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw a donkey branded on the face, and he disapproved, and the man said: 'By Allah, I will not brand it except on the farthest part of the face.' So he ordered his donkey to be branded on its buttocks. He was the first to brand on the buttocks." Al-Ṭabarānī added: "The man who branded was al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.") So he branded her on her buttocks. (*Juwāʿir*: the area around the anus, according to al-Ṣiḥāḥ. ʿ)

As for the word *al-khurṭūm* (snout): it is contempt and disdain for him.

It is also said that its meaning is: "We will mark him on the Day of Resurrection with a disfiguring sign by which he will be distinguished from the rest of the disbelievers, just as he (the Prophet) (ﷺ) opposed him with an enmity by which he distinguished himself from them."

It is also said: he was struck on the snout with a sword on the Day of Badr, and a mark remained on his snout.

It is also said: "We will make him notorious for this insult in both abodes, so it will not be hidden, just as a mark on the snout is not hidden."

From al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl: *al-khurṭūm* means wine, and its meaning is "We will punish him with the prescribed punishment for drinking it." This is far-fetched. Wine is also called *al-khurṭūm*, just as it is called *al-sulāfah*, which is what has passed of grape juice. Or it is because it flies into the nostrils (*al-khayāshīm*).

**Mashshā'in bi-namīm**: one who carries tales, transmitting speech from one people to another, with the intent of stirring up mischief and discord between them. *Al-namīm* and *al-namīmah* mean incitement and tale-bearing. (Al-Sihāḥ says: "*al-tadrīb bayn al-qawm*" means stirring enmity.) (ʿ)

Some Arabs recited to me:

*"Flare up, as the tale-bearing flares up,*
*Walking with it, Zahrā, to Tamīm."*

This is said by a Bedouin addressing the fire. *Al-tashabbub* means kindling. *Al-tamīmah* means the distortion and embellishment of speech to cause discord among people. A garment that is *munammam* or *munamnam* is one decorated with patterns or made fine. Zahrā, with a fatḥah, is the name of a tale-bearing woman. Tamīm is the tribe of Tamīm. He made the fire occupy the place of a reasonable being, commanded it, and said: "Flare up like the flaring of tale-bearing, while this woman walks with it to the Banū Tamīm." She was very active in causing discord among the Arabs, so that she became proverbial. He made the flaring of her tale-bearing more intense than the flaring of fire, so he commanded it to blaze as she blazes. Between *namīm* and *tamīmah* there is *jinās lāḥiq* (a near-paronomasia). (ʿ)

**Mannāʿ lil-khayr**: stingy. *Al-khayr* means wealth. Or *mannāʿ* means one who withholds the good for his family, and the good is Islam. So he mentioned the one prevented from it instead of the thing prevented, as if he said: "one who withholds from the good."

It is said he is al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra al-Makhzūmī. He was wealthy and had ten sons. He would say to them and to his kin: "Whoever among you embraces Islam, I will withhold my bounty from him."

From Ibn ʿAbbās: he is Abū Jahl.

From Mujāhid: al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth.

From al-Suddī: al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, whose origin was among Thaqīf, but whose affiliation was with Zuhra. For this reason it is said he is a *zanīm*.

**Muʿtadin**: exceeding the bounds in wrongdoing.

**Athīm**: much sinful, committing many sins.

**ʿUtull**: harsh, coarse, rough. From *ʿatalahu*: when one drags him with violence and roughness.

**Baʿda dhālika**: after he was described with the defects and shortcomings mentioned above.

**Zanīm**: an illegitimate, adopted one. (The author Maḥmūd said: "*al-ʿutull* is the coarse one, and *al-zanīm* is the illegitimate claimant. Likewise al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra was adopted by al-Mughīra eighteen years after his birth…" Aḥmad said: "He took these two to be the worst of his defects from his words *baʿda dhālik*, for it indicates a distance in rank between what was mentioned first and what was mentioned after it, in evil and in good. Its counterpart in good is His saying: ﴿and the angels after that are supporters﴾. For this reason *thumma* is used to express the distance in ranks, even though it gives the reverse of the existential order.") (ʿ)

Ḥassān said:

*"You are a zanīm, hung to the family of Hāshim,*
*As a lone arrow is hung behind the rider."*

This is addressed by Ḥassān ibn Thābit to al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra. He says that he is *zanīm*, that is, attached to the family of Hāshim like the *zunmah* on a hide, which is a small piece of skin left hanging at its edge. He compared him to it, and compared him to the empty, lone arrow hung behind the rider. (ʿ)

Al-Walīd was an adopted outsider among the Quraysh, not of their stock. His father claimed him eighteen years after his birth.

It is also said: his mother committed adultery, and this was not known until this verse was revealed. He made his coarseness and his being claimed by another the worst of his defects, because when a man is coarse and his nature is harsh, his heart hardens and he becomes bold in every sin. Also, the general rule is that when the seed is corrupt, what comes from it is corrupt.

For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The child of fornication will not enter Paradise, nor his child, nor his child's child." (Abū Nuʿaym narrated it in the biography of Mujāhid, through ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥasan, in the biography of Yūsuf ibn Asbāṭ, through Barakah ibn Muḥammad, from Yūsuf ibn Asbāṭ, from Abū Isrāʾīl al-Malāʾī, from Ismāʿīl ibn Isḥāq, from Qabīṣah ibn ʿAmr, from Mujāhid, from Banī ʿUmar, from Abū Hurayrah. Then he narrated it through Isḥāq ibn Manṣūr from Abū Isrāʾīl with the same wording, but Abū Isrāʾīl is extremely weak. Ibn Ṭāhir and Ibn al-Jawzī claimed that this hadith is fabricated. It has been contradicted on the authority of Mujāhid: al-Nasāʾī narrated it through Ibrāhīm ibn Mujāhid, from Mujāhid, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Abū Hurayrah, with the wording: "The child of fornication will not enter Paradise, nor anything of his offspring up to seven fathers," but Ibrāhīm is weak in it. He also narrated it through Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād, from Mujāhid, from Abū Saʿīd, similar to the hadith of Manṣūr that follows, but Yazīd is weak. Al-Nasāʾī also narrated through Shuʿbah, from Manṣūr, from Sālim ibn Abī al-Jaʿd, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sharīk, from Jābān, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, with the wording: "The child of an adulteress will not enter Paradise," and through Sufyān, from Manṣūr, dropping ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sharīk. Ibn Ḥibbān narrated it through both channels, and said: "Both channels are preserved, but al-Thawrī is more knowledgeable about the hadith of Manṣūr.")

**Baʿda dhālik** is similar to *thumma* in His saying: ﴿then he was among those who believed﴾.

Al-Ḥasan read *ʿutullin* with a *ḍammah* (in the nominative), as a form of disparagement. This reading strengthens what is indicated by what comes after.

**Zanīm**: from *al-zunmah*, which is a small piece of flesh from a she-goat's hide, cut off and left hanging from its throat. He is an addition hung on someone who does not belong to him.

**An kāna dhā māl**: this is connected to His saying: ﴿and do not obey﴾. That is, do not obey him with these defects, because he possesses wealth. That is, because of his prosperity and his share of this world. It is also permissible that it be connected to what follows, meaning: because he is wealthy and is supported by sons ﴿who denies Our signs﴾. (The phrase "who denies Our signs" is in al-Nasafī's wording: "denies with Our signs." ʿ) It is not governed by *qāla* (he says), which is the answer of *idhā* (when), because what follows a conditional does not govern what precedes it. Rather, what governs it is the meaning of denial that the sentence indicates.

It is read *a-an kāna*? (with the interrogative hamzah), as an interrogation: "Is it because he possesses wealth and sons that he denies?" Or: "Would you obey him because he possesses wealth?"

Al-Zubayrī narrated from Nāfiʿ: *in kāna* with a kasrah, with the conditional applied to the addressee. That is: do not obey every oath-maker who stipulates his prosperity, because if you obey the disbeliever for his wealth, it is as if you made wealth a condition for obedience. Diverting the conditional to the addressee is like diverting the expectation (*tarajjī*) to him in His saying: ﴿perhaps he will be reminded﴾.

**The nose** (*al-wajh*, the face, the nose): The nose is the most honored part of the body, and the nose is the most honored part of the face because it is foremost in it. For this reason they made it the place of honor and zeal, and derived from it *al-anfah* (pride). They said: "The nose is in the nose," "he protected his nose," and "so-and-so has a lofty nose." And for the humiliated they said: "his nose was slit," and "his nose was rubbed in the dust." So he expressed the utmost humiliation and disgrace by branding on the snout, because a mark on the face is a disfigurement and a debasement. How much more so when it is on the most honored part of it! The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) branded al-ʿAbbās's camels on their faces, and he said to him: "Honor the faces." (I have not seen it in this exact form. In Ibn Ḥibbān, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, that al-ʿAbbās branded a camel of his and a beast on its face, and the Prophet (ﷺ) saw it and was angry. Al-ʿAbbās said: "I will not brand it except at its far end." So he branded it on its buttocks. Its origin is in Muslim with the wording: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw a donkey branded on the face, and he disapproved, and the man said: 'By Allah, I will not brand it except on the farthest part of the face.' So he ordered his donkey to be branded on its buttocks. He was the first to brand on the buttocks." Al-Ṭabarānī added: "The man who branded was al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.") So he branded her on her buttocks. (*Juwāʿir*: the area around the anus, according to al-Ṣiḥāḥ. ʿ)

As for the word *al-khurṭūm* (snout): it is contempt and disdain for him.

It is also said that its meaning is: "We will mark him on the Day of Resurrection with a disfiguring sign by which he will be distinguished from the rest of the disbelievers, just as he (the Prophet) (ﷺ) opposed him with an enmity by which he distinguished himself from them."

It is also said: he was struck on the snout with a sword on the Day of Badr, and a mark remained on his snout.

It is also said: "We will make him notorious for this insult in both abodes, so it will not be hidden, just as a mark on the snout is not hidden."

From al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl: *al-khurṭūm* means wine, and its meaning is "We will punish him with the prescribed punishment for drinking it." This is far-fetched. Wine is also called *al-khurṭūm*, just as it is called *al-sulāfah*, which is what has passed of grape juice. Or it is because it flies into the nostrils (*al-khayāshīm*).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 68, verses 17–33:

We have tested the people of Makkah with famine and hunger, in response to the supplication of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) against them, ﴿as We tested the people of the garden﴾. They were a people from among the followers of prayer (ahl al-salah). Their father owned this garden, two farsakhs (about six miles) from Sana'a. [[Mahmud said: "The people of the garden were a people from among the followers of prayer, whose father owned this garden two farsakhs from Sana'a..." etc. Ahmad said: The purpose of using the indefinite form (al-tankir) is to convey vagueness, to magnify what befell it. The meaning of ﴿like the dark (al-sarim)﴾ is: due to the destruction of its fruit. It was also said that al-sarim means the night, because it was burnt and blackened. It was also said that it means the day, i.e., empty and bare, from the saying "bayyada al-ina'" when one empties the vessel. I say: from this comes the word bayad, meaning barren land, i.e., land free of trees. It occurs in a hadith, and the jurists use it in the context of musaqah (an agreement for irrigating and tending trees in exchange for a share of the produce). The meaning of ﴿harvesting (sarimin)﴾ is reaping.

He said: The phrase ﴿upon your tilth﴾ uses ʿala rather than ila because their going out in the morning was for the purpose of harvesting it, so it is a going out "upon" it. The meaning of ﴿they whispered (yatakhafatun)﴾ is that they spoke their conversation secretly, out of fear that the poor would see them. His words ﴿that no poor man shall enter it today against you﴾ are like saying "I shall not see you here." The word harad comes from "haradat al-sanah," when the year withholds its goodness. The meaning is: they went out in the morning in distress and deprivation, not unable to benefit. It was also said that harad means swiftness, i.e., they went out quickly and eagerly, resolved to deprive others. The meaning of ﴿able (qadirin)﴾ on this interpretation is: in their own estimation. It was also said that harad is the name of the garden mentioned. Their words ﴿indeed we are astray﴾ were said in the immediacy of their situation, bewildered, because they saw something they were not used to, so they believed they had lost their way to it and that this was not it. Then, when they realized and became certain that it was indeed it, they turned away from the first statement to their words ﴿rather we are deprived﴾.]] He used to take from it the provision for his year and give away the remainder in charity. He would leave for the poor whatever the sickle missed, what was at the bottom of the heaps (al-akdas), and what the pickers missed of the grapes, and what remained on the cloth spread beneath the palm when it was harvested. Much would accumulate for them. When he died, his sons said: If we do what our father used to do, the matter will be too tight for us, and we are people with dependents. So they swore that they would harvest it at dawn, in the darkness (al-sadaf), secretly from the poor, and they did not make an exception (istithna') in their oath. So God burned their garden. It was also said that they were from the Children of Israel. ﴿Going out at dawn﴾ means entering the morning early, ﴿and they did not make exception﴾ means they did not say "if God wills."

If you ask: why is it called an exception when it is a condition? I answer: because it performs the function of an exception, in that the meaning of your saying "I will certainly go out, if God wills" is the same as "I will not go out unless God wills."

﴿A calamity from your Lord encircled it while they were asleep﴾, i.e., a misfortune or destruction (ta'if), like His saying: ﴿and it was encompassed (wa-uhita) by its fruit﴾. It was also read as tayf. ﴿So it became like the dark (al-sarim)﴾, like a harvested field, due to the destruction of its fruit. It was also said that al-sarim is the night, i.e., it was burnt and blackened. It was also said that it is the day, i.e., it dried up and its greenness went away, or nothing was left in it, from the saying "bayyada al-ina'" when one empties the vessel. It was also said that al-sarim means sand dunes. ﴿Harvesting (sarimin)﴾ means reaping.

If you ask: why was it not said "go out to your tilth," and what is the meaning of ʿala? I answer: since going out to it was for the purpose of harvesting and cutting it, it became a going out "upon" it, just as you say "the enemy went out upon them (ghada ʿalayhim al-ʿaduwwu)." It is also permissible that going out (al-ghadw) contains the meaning of approaching (al-iqbal), as in the saying: "He is brought to him (yughda ʿalayhi) with the bowl in the morning and in the evening." That is: approach your tilth early in the morning.

﴿They whispered (yatakhafatun)﴾ means they spoke secretly among themselves. The roots kha-fa-ya, kha-fa-ta, and kha-fa-da all carry the sense of concealing, and from this comes al-khaftad, the name for the bat. ﴿That (an) no poor man shall enter it﴾: the an here is explanatory (mufassirah). Ibn Mas'ud read it without the particle, with the verb of saying implied: "they whispered, saying: no poor man shall enter it." The prohibition on the poor entering is a prohibition on giving them the means to enter, i.e., do not enable them to enter so that they enter, like your saying "I shall not see you here." Harad: from "haradat al-sanah," when the year withholds its goodness, and "haradat al-ibil," when the camels withhold their milk. The meaning is: they went out able to cause distress, not unable to benefit. That is, they resolved to distress the poor and deprive them, while they were able to benefit them. So they went out in a state of poverty and loss of wealth, in which they were able only to cause distress and deprivation, because they had sought to deprive the poor, so deprivation and poverty were hastened upon them. Or: they went out withholding their garden and the loss of its goodness, able, instead of being able to reap its goodness and benefits; that is, they went out obtaining deprivation instead of benefit. Or: when they said "go out to your tilth," while their intention had become corrupt, God punished them by withholding their garden and depriving them of its goodness, so they did not go out to a tilth but to a harad. The word "able (qadirin)" is used in reverse for mockery (tahakkum): able to do what they had resolved concerning harvesting and depriving the poor, and "upon harad" is not related to "able." It was also said: harad has the meaning of harad (the same).

It was read ʿala harad, meaning they were able only to rage and anger, some against others, like His saying: ﴿they blame one another (yatalawamuna)﴾. It was also said that harad means intention and haste, as one says "haradta hardaka" (go at your own pace). And a poet said:

"A torrent came, sent by God's command... it rushes like a garden that is fruitful and abundant."

He describes the torrent as abundant, which is why he said "from God's command." It is also narrated as "min amr Allah," and the alif before the ha' in the word Allah was dropped, because that is permissible in pausal form. Harad, yahrud, is of the pattern ḍaraba, meaning to aim for and hasten, i.e., it hastens with the haste of the garden, i.e., the orchard, which is abundant in yield and goodness. The meaning of the haste of the garden is that its goodness appears before others within a short time. He chose it because it arises from the torrent.

Qata harad means swift (sira'): the meaning is: they went out hastily and energetically toward their garden, able in their own estimation, saying: we are able to harvest it and to withhold its benefit from the poor. It was also said that harad is a name for the garden, i.e., they went out upon that garden able to harvest it in their own estimation, or determined that their aim of harvesting and depriving would be accomplished. ﴿They said, when they arrived (fi badihat wusulihim)﴾: ﴿indeed we are astray﴾, meaning: we have lost our garden, and this is not it, because they saw its destruction. When they reflected and knew that it was it, they said: ﴿rather we are deprived﴾, deprived of its goodness because of our own transgression against ourselves.

﴿The best of them (awsatuhum)﴾, i.e., the most just and best of them, from the saying "he is of the middle (sitah) of his people" and "give me from the middle (sata) of your wealth." From this is His saying: ﴿a middle nation (ummatan wasatan)﴾. ﴿Why do you not glorify (lawla tusabbihun)﴾, i.e., why do you not remember God and turn to Him from the corruption of your intention. It is as if their best among them said to them when they resolved upon that: remember God and His retribution against the criminals, repent of this corrupt resolve at once, and hasten to cut off its evil before the vengeance comes. But they disobeyed him, so he rebuked them. The evidence for this is their saying: ﴿Glory be to our Lord, indeed we were wrongdoers﴾. So they spoke with what had been calling them to speak immediately after committing the sin, but only after the ruin of the garden. It was also said: the intended meaning of glorification (tasbih) is the exception (istithna'), because both share the sense of exalting God, since the exception is entrusting the matter to Him, and glorification is declaring Him free of imperfection, and each of entrusting and declaring-free is an exaltation. It is narrated from al-Hasan that it means prayer, as if they had been negligent in prayer, for otherwise it would have forbidden them from indecency and wrongdoing, and it would have been a kindness for them to make the exception and not deprive. ﴿Glory be to our Lord﴾: they glorified God and declared Him free of injustice and every ugliness, then acknowledged their own wrongdoing in withholding what is good and in omitting the exception. ﴿They blamed one another (yatalawamuna)﴾, each blaming the other, because some of them had urged, some had accepted, some had commanded restraint and gave an excuse, some had disobeyed the command, and some had remained silent while approving. ﴿That He may give us in exchange (an yubdilana)﴾ is read with doubling and without. ﴿To our Lord we are eager (raghibun)﴾, seeking good from Him, hoping for His pardon.

﴿Thus is the punishment﴾, like that punishment with which We tested the people of Makkah and the people of the garden, the punishment of this world. ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is greater (wa-la-ʿadhabu al-akhirati akbar)﴾, more severe and greater than it.

Qatadah was asked about the people of the garden: are they among the people of Paradise or of the Fire? He said: You have burdened me with a difficult question.

It is narrated from Mujahid: they repented, and so God gave them better than it. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him: It has reached me that they were sincere, and God recognized their truthfulness, so He gave them in its place a garden called al-Hayawan (the Living), in which there are grapes, and a mule could carry one bunch of them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 68, verses 35–39:

The chieftains of Quraysh used to see their abundant share of this world and the scarcity of the Muslims' share of it. So when they heard about the Hereafter and what Allah had promised the Muslims, they would say: "If it is true that we will be resurrected, as Muhammad and those with him claim, then their state and ours will be no different from what it is in this world. Otherwise they would not surpass us or be superior to us, and at best their situation would be equal to ours." So it was said: "Shall We treat the Muslims like the disbelievers?" Then they were addressed, by way of iltifat (shift of address) [[Mahmud said: "This is an address in the manner of iltifat to the people of Mecca, when they believe that in the Hereafter they will have greater bliss than the believers... etc." Ahmad said: And since the lesson was a statement, he broke it.]]: "What is wrong with you? How do you judge? This is a crooked judgment, as if the matter of recompense were entrusted to you, so that you judge about it as you wish. Or do you have a Book from heaven in which you study that what you choose and desire is yours?" Like His saying, "Or do you have a clear authority? Then bring your book" (37:156–157). The original reading is "tadrusuna anna lakum ma takhayyarun," with anna opened, because it is the object of study; when the lam came, it was made kasra. It is also permissible that it be a quotation of what is studied, as it is, like His saying, "And We left for him among the later generations: Peace upon Noah among the worlds" (37:78–79). Takhayyara al-shay' and ikhtarahu: he took its best part. Similar to it: tanakhala and intankhala, when one takes its choicest part (minkhul). "Li-fulan 'alayya yamin bi-kadha": when I have guaranteed him something from it and sworn to him on fulfilling it, meaning: "Or have We taken a guarantee from you and sworn to you oaths, emphatic and fully confirmed in assertion?" [[His saying "idha darntahu minhu wa halaftu lahu" is perhaps "'anhu" (from him), and likewise his saying "minkum" is perhaps "'ankum" (from you). In the Sihah: "daminatuhu al-shay' tadminan fa-tadammanahu 'anhu" (I made him responsible for the thing and he became responsible for it from me). (Ayn)]]

If you ask: "What does ila yawm al-qiyamah (until the Day of Resurrection) relate to?" I say: it relates to what is implied in the adverb, meaning: "It is established for you against Us until the Day of Resurrection; you will not be released from its obligation except on that day, when We judge you and give you what you judge for." It is also permissible that it relate to *baligha* (fully reaching), meaning that it reaches that day and ends at it, complete, with no oath of it nullified until the sworn matter is fulfilled through the judgment. Al-Hasan read *baligha* in the accusative, as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in the adverb. "Inna lakum lama tahkumun" is the answer to the oath, because the meaning of "Or do you have oaths binding on Us" is "Or have We sworn to you?"

It is also read *tukshafu* with a *tāʾ* and a *ḍamma* on the first letter and a *kasra* on the *shīn*, from *akshafa*, meaning "to enter into uncovering." From this comes *akshafa al-rajulu*, "the man became one whose upper lip is turned back," when his upper lip is everted.

The adverbial complement of time (*nāṣib al-ẓarf*) is *fa-l-yaʾtū* (﴿let them bring their partners﴾, 68:41). Or it is governed by an implied *udhkur*, "remember," or the sense is: "on the day when the shin is uncovered, there will be such and such," and it is omitted for emphatic terror, since there are among the events things that cannot be described because of their magnitude.

From Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him: "their spines will be made rigid," meaning they will be turned into bones without joints, which do not bend when raised or lowered. In the ḥadīth: "their spines will remain one single layer," meaning one single vertebra.

If you ask: why are they called to prostration when there is no obligation? The answer: they are not called to it as an act of worship and obligation, but as a rebuke and reproach for their refusal to prostrate in the world, while their spines are made rigid and a barrier is placed between them and the capacity to prostrate, as a cause of regret and remorse for what they neglected when they were called to prostration, while their spines and joints were sound and they were able, free from impediments, to fulfil what they had been commanded to do [[His words "wa-hum sālimūna al-aṣlāb": he may mean *sālimū al-aṣlāb* with the genitive construction. (ʿA.)]].

"It is said: Leave Me with the one who denies this discourse" — they mean: entrust him to Me, for I will suffice you against him. As if He says: "It is enough for you to bring about his ruin that you leave his affair to Me and leave between Me and him; for I am acting in accordance with what ought to be done to him, and I am capable of it." The intended meaning is: "My being sufficient as a recompender of the one who denies the Qur'an" [[His saying "and the intended meaning is: My being sufficient as a recompender" — the familiar usage is: "Sufficient for you is Me as recompenser," or "Sufficient for you is God as recompenser." (Ibn al-Munir? / the glossator)]]. So do not occupy your heart with his affair, and rely upon Me for taking vengeance on him, as consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and as a threat to the deniers.

"Istadraja-hu ila kadha" (he drew him on to such-and-such): when he brings him down to it step by step, until he entangles him in it. The "istidraj" (gradual enticement) of Allah toward the disobedient is that He grants them health and blessing, so that they make the provision of Allah a means and a ladder to an increase in unbelief and sins, "from where they do not know" (min haythu la ya'lamun), i.e., from the direction in which they do not perceive that it is an enticement, which is the bestowal of favours upon them, because they consider it a preference for them and an elevation over the believers, whereas it is the cause of their destruction. "And I give them respite" (wa umli lahum): I grant them time, like His saying, Exalted is He: "We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin" (innama numli lahum li-yazdadu ithma). Health, provision and the lengthening of life are a kindness and bounty from Allah which obliges them to gratitude and obedience, but they make it a cause of unbelief by their own choice; so when they progressed through it to destruction, He described the Benefactor as the one who entices (istidraj). It is said: How many are enticed by kindness shown to them, how many are beguiled by praise bestowed upon them, and how many are deceived by being covered over (by God's concealment of their faults). He named His kindness and enablement "kayd" (scheming), just as He named it "istidraj", because it takes the form of scheming, since it became the cause of their entanglement in ruin; and He described it as "matin" (firm/mighty) because of the strength of the effect of His kindness in causing their destruction.

It is a good idiom to make the verb masculine because the pronoun is separated, in (تداركه). Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud read (تداركته). Al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 68, verses 51–52:

Inna (إن) is the lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy form (al-thaqila), and the lam after it is its marker (lam 'alamaha).

It is also read as "liyuzliqunaka" with the yaa' vowelled with a damma and with a fatha. Zalaqahu and azlaqahu have the same meaning. It is said: zalaqa al-ra's wa azlaqahu: he shaved the head.

It is also read as "liyuzhiqunaka," from zahaqat nafsuhu and azhaqaha (the soul departed / he caused it to depart), meaning:

Because of the intensity of their staring and their looking at you sidelong with eyes of enmity and hatred, they nearly make your foot slip or destroy you. This is from their saying: "He looked at me with a look that nearly throws me down (yasra'uni)," and "a look that nearly eats me," meaning: if his look were able to cause a fall or to devour, he would do it. The poet said:

They exchange glances when they meet in a place, glances that make the feet of walkers slip.

[[He says: when they meet in an assembly (and it is narrated as "mawțin"): "yataqaradun" means that each gives the other a glance, as if one of them offers his opponent a look and the other returns it with a look out of envy and rage. "Izlal mawati' al-aqdam" (causing the feet's footing to slip) is a metaphor for destruction, because whoever's foot slips falls to the ground and may perish. That is: they look at one another with the gaze of the envious, enraged person, so the feet slip from their places; and attributing the slipping to the places of the feet is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), since it is their locus, and in it there is exaggeration regarding the slipping of the foot.]]

It is also said: the evil eye was among the Banu Asad. A man among them would go hungry for three days so that nothing would pass by him, and then he would say about someone: "I have never seen a day like today, except that it harmed him (eaanahu)." Then some of those afflicted by the evil eye were brought to him, so that he would say the same about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: "I have never seen a man like today," but Allah protected him.

From al-Hasan: the cure for being afflicted by the evil eye is to recite this verse: "When they heard the Reminder" (lamma sami'u al-dhikr), i.e., the Qur'an, "they could not control themselves out of envy for what you were given of prophethood, and they say: 'Indeed, he is a madman'" (wa yaqulun innahu lamajnun), out of bewilderment regarding his affair and to repel people from him, though they knew he was the most intelligent of them. The meaning is:

They declared him mad because of the Qur'an, "and it is not but a reminder and admonition to the worlds" (wa ma huwa illa dhikrun wa mawizatun lil-'alamin), so how could one be called mad who brought its like?

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Qalam, Allah will grant him the reward of those whose character Allah has made good."
